t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we learn to detect thallium, zinc, antimony and cadmium cations in the mineralisate. The work is connected with quantitative analysis by the PEC method. Aim: to become familiar with the toxicological significance and methods of analysis of metallic poisons isolated by mineralisation with sulphuric and nitric acids. The expected outcome is that you will be able to detect in the filtrate the cations that may be present in the mineralisate.

The following are needed for the session: mineralisate, filter paper, funnel, reagents, test tubes, demonstration materials, adhesive tape and paper. The session takes place in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. In the methods, a separatory funnel, universal indicator, microscope and microscope slide are used. During the reactions we shall turn to each of these items.

t: Session map: Tl, Zn, Sb, Cd and Bi
n: This is the session map. Thallium, zinc, antimony and cadmium are detected in the mineralisate, and bismuth is also considered. For thallium, malachite green and thallium(I) dithizonate are used. For zinc, the dithizone reaction, separation with diethyldithiocarbamate (DDTC), and the sulphide, ferrocyanide and microcrystalline reactions are carried out. For antimony, malachite green and sulphide are used; for cadmium, separation with DDTC, sulphide, copper ferrocyanide and brucine. For bismuth, the reactions with thiourea, 8-hydroxyquinoline, that is, oxine, separation with DDTC and microcrystalline reactions are carried out.

We begin with the reaction forming the complex of thallium with malachite green. To 1 ml of mineralisate, 4 ml of 40% H2SO4, 3 ml of 5N HCl, 2 drops of 5% NaNO2, 7 drops of 0.5% malachite green, Na2SO4 and 5 ml of toluene are added. If antimony or thallium is present, the toluene layer is coloured sky blue and the aqueous layer yellow-brown. This colour is the same for both cations.

t: Malachite green: testing the toluene layer
n: Testing the toluene layer. The toluene layer is separated, 3 ml of 25% sulphuric acid is added, and the mixture is shaken for 5 seconds. If the colour persists, the toluene layer is coloured by the complex of antimony or thallium with malachite green. But with this reaction it is difficult to tell which of the two, antimony or thallium, is present. For this reason one more reaction is recommended for thallium.

The reagents of the malachite green reaction. In a separatory funnel, 4 ml of 40% H2SO4 and 3 ml of 5N HCl are added to 1 ml of mineralisate. Then 2 drops of 5% sodium nitrite, 7 drops of 0.5% malachite green, 1-2 g of anhydrous Na2SO4 and 5 ml of toluene are added. The mixture is stirred thoroughly for 1-2 minutes. As a result the toluene layer is coloured sky blue and the aqueous layer yellow-brown.

The thallium(I) dithizonate complex. To 5 ml of mineralisate, 10% ammonia is added under universal-indicator control until pH 12-13. Then 3 ml of chloroform and a few drops of 0.1% dithizone, as a solution in chloroform, are added, shaken strongly and allowed to settle. If thallium compounds are present, a bluish-violet colour forms in the chloroform layer.

We compare two reactions for thallium. With malachite green the toluene layer is coloured sky blue, but this reaction is the same for antimony and thallium. For this reason the reaction forming thallium(I) dithizonate is recommended for thallium. In the dithizone reaction, at pH 12-13 the chloroform layer becomes bluish-violet. In the table the medium, layer and result are shown side by side.

Now zinc. The first stage is the dithizonate reaction, the preliminary test. 0.5 ml of mineralisate and 0.5 ml of saturated thiosulphate are mixed and brought to pH 4.5-5.0, and 1 ml of pH 5 acetate buffer is added. Then 2 drops of 0.01% dithizone in chloroform and 1 ml of chloroform are added and mixed thoroughly. If zinc is present, the chloroform is coloured red-violet. If there is no colour, no other tests are carried out for zinc.

The key values for zinc dithizonate. To 0.5 ml of mineralisate, 0.5 ml of saturated sodium thiosulphate is added and the mixture is brought to pH 4.5-5.0. Then 1 ml of pH 5 acetate buffer, 2 drops of 0.01% dithizone in chloroform and 1 ml of chloroform are added. If zinc is present, the chloroform layer is coloured red-violet. Remember these values exactly, as in the table.

Isolating zinc with DDTC. To 10 ml of mineralisate, 4 ml of 20% citric acid and 1 ml of saturated thiourea, or thiosulphate, are added, and the pH is brought to 8.5 with 10% KOH. Then 3 ml of 1% sodium diethyldithiocarbamate and 5 ml of chloroform are added and shaken for 1-2 minutes. The yellow-brown chloroform layer is separated: it contains zinc diethyldithiocarbamate. It is then re-extracted with 3 ml of 1N HCl and the qualitative reactions are carried out.

Re-extraction and qualitative reactions. The chloroform extract is shaken with 3 ml of 1N HCl, and the zinc reactions are carried out in the aqueous part. In the sulphide reaction, 10% KOH is added to pH 5, and then 3-4 drops of fresh Na2S are added; if zinc is present, a white precipitate forms. In the ferrocyanide reaction, 10% NaOH is added to pH 5, then 3-4 drops of 5% K ferrocyanide; here too a white precipitate appears.

t: Zinc and cadmium: comparing separation with DDTC
n: We compare the sequence of separating zinc and cadmium with DDTC. For zinc, with 4 ml of 20% citric acid, at pH 8.5, the mixture is shaken for 1-2 minutes with 3 ml of 1% DDTC and 5 ml of chloroform. For cadmium, 2 ml of 10% glycerol, 4 ml of 10% Rochelle salt and Nile blue are used; then the mixture is shaken with 3 ml of 1% DDTC and 10 ml of chloroform for 30 minutes. In both cases the chloroform layer is re-extracted with 3 ml of 1N HCl.

The microcrystalloscopic reaction for zinc. 1-2 drops of the solution are placed on a microscope slide and dried. The dry residue is dissolved in 1 drop of 10% acetic acid, and 1 drop of ammonium tetrathiocyanatomercurate salt solution is added on top. After a few minutes, dendrite-shaped microcrystals are observed under the microscope. The shape of the crystals is drawn in the laboratory notebook.

The reaction of antimony with malachite green. In a separatory funnel, to 1 ml of mineralisate, 4 ml of 40% H2SO4, 3 ml of 5N HCl, 2 drops of 5% NaNO2, 7 drops of 0.5% malachite green, Na2SO4 and 5 ml of toluene are added. It is stirred for 1-2 minutes: if antimony or thallium is present, the toluene layer is coloured sky blue. If, when the toluene layer is shaken with 3 ml of 25% H2SO4 for 5 seconds, the colour persists, the reaction is considered positive.

t: Antimony: assessing the result and the sulphide reaction
n: Assessing the antimony result. If the malachite green reaction is negative, the examination for antimony is stopped; otherwise additional confirmation is mandatory. In the antimony sulphide reaction, 5 drops of saturated sodium thiosulphate are added to 10 ml of mineralisate and boiled for 1-2 minutes. If antimony is present, a yellow-brown precipitate forms.

How do antimony and thallium differ? The malachite green reaction is the same for both: the toluene layer is coloured sky blue. The additional reaction for thallium is thallium(I) dithizonate: at pH 12-13 the chloroform becomes bluish-violet. The additional reaction for antimony is boiling with sodium thiosulphate for 1-2 minutes: a yellow-brown precipitate forms. Thus, the distinguishing feature lies precisely in the additional reaction.

Separating cadmium with DDTC. To 10 ml of mineralisate, 2 ml of 10% glycerol, 4 ml of 10% Rochelle salt and 0.1% Nile blue as indicator are added. Then 2.5N NaOH is added dropwise until a reddish colour. Then the mixture is shaken for 30 minutes with 3 ml of 1% DDTC and 10 ml of chloroform. The lower chloroform portion is separated and shaken with 3 ml of 1N HCl; this is called re-extraction.

t: Cadmium: values for separation with DDTC
n: Values for separating cadmium with DDTC. 10 ml of mineralisate is mixed with 2 ml of 10% glycerol, 4 ml of 10% Rochelle salt and 1-2 drops of 0.1% Nile blue. 2.5N sodium hydroxide is added until the liquid turns reddish. Then the mixture is shaken strongly for 30 minutes with 3 ml of 1% sodium diethyldithiocarbamate and 10 ml of chloroform. Note that the shaking time is considerably longer than in the case of zinc.

Reactions confirming cadmium. To the re-extract, 10% alkali is added to pH 5, then 3-4 drops of 5% sodium sulphide: if cadmium is present, a yellow precipitate forms. This sulphide reaction gives a positive result when the amount of cadmium in the solution is above 50 µg. In the cadmium and copper ferrocyanide reaction, 10 drops of 2% CuSO4 and 1-2 drops of 5% K ferrocyanide are added; a pale violet precipitate forms. With KBr and brucine or pyridine, colourless prismatic crystals separate.

The reaction scheme of cadmium sulphide. Reagents: 1 ml of re-extract, brought to pH 5 with 10% sodium or potassium alkali, and 3-4 drops of 5% Na2S. The product is a yellow precipitate. Remember: the reaction gives a positive result when the amount of cadmium is above 50 µg, that is, with a very small amount the precipitate may not be visible.

Now bismuth. First of all, reactions with thiourea and 8-hydroxyquinoline are carried out with bismuth. If saturated thiourea is added to 5 ml of mineralisate, a lemon-yellow solution forms; oxidants interfere. With oxine, a yellow-orange colour belongs to oxine iodobismuthate; a mixture of acetone and amyl acetate makes the layer reddish-orange. The table gives the purpose of the reagents: ascorbic acid masks Fe3+, Rochelle salt masks Cu2+, potassium iodide removes oxidants.

Separating bismuth with DDTC. If the reactions are not positive, the analysis of the mineralisate for bismuth is stopped. With a positive result, bismuth is extracted with the help of diethyldithiocarbamate and identified by additional reactions. 10 ml of mineralisate and Nile blue are placed in a separatory funnel and made alkaline with NaOH until a red-pink colour, pH = 12. On shaking with sodium diethyldithiocarbamate and 5 ml of chloroform, brown Bi(DDTC)3 passes into the chloroform layer, which is then shaken with nitric acid solution.

Microcrystalline reactions of bismuth. If crystals of caesium chloride and potassium iodide are added, hexagonal red-orange crystals of composition Cs2BiJ5 form. If solutions of brucine and KBr are added, green spheroid-shaped microcrystals are seen, owing to H2BiBr5·2brucine. The shape of the crystals is drawn in the laboratory notebook, and the results are interpreted according to the requirements of forensic chemistry.

We summarise the results. Thallium is detected with dithizone at pH 12-13, and the chloroform becomes bluish-violet. Zinc is detected with dithizone at pH 4.5-5.0, and the chloroform becomes red-violet. Antimony and cadmium are confirmed by precipitation reactions: with antimony, a yellow-brown precipitate on boiling with sodium thiosulphate; with cadmium, a yellow precipitate with Na2S at pH 5.

t: If the first reaction is negative
n: What is done if the first reaction is negative? If the malachite green reaction is negative, the examination for antimony is stopped; otherwise additional confirmation is mandatory. If no colour forms with dithizone, the mineralisate is not tested further for zinc. If the bismuth reactions do not give a positive result, the analysis of the mineralisate for bismuth is stopped. This rule saves unnecessary work and makes the analysis systematic.

The pH conditions differ by cation. For thallium dithizonate pH 12-13, for zinc dithizonate pH 4.5-5.0. In separating zinc with DDTC the pH is 8.5; the sulphide and ferrocyanide reactions proceed at pH 5. Cadmium sulphide forms in the re-extract at pH 5. In separating bismuth with DDTC, the mineralisate is made alkaline with NaOH until a red-pink colour, pH = 12. For this reason it is important to control the pH precisely with universal indicator.

The Venn diagram is used to compare 2-3 aspects and their common features; it develops skills of systematic thinking and analysis. The diagram in the book shows circles for cadmium, bismuth and antimony. In small groups the diagram is constructed, and the non-overlapping places are filled in with an x. Then the results are compared in pairs.

t: Case 11: haemorrhages in the lungs and oesophagus
n: Now a case. The internal organs of a corpse were brought to forensic chemical examination. Pathological examination showed signs of haemorrhage in the lung tissue and oesophagus, and nephritis in the kidney. Task: to explain the cause and the solution of the case and to carry out the forensic chemical analysis.

Situational problem. At an enterprise, chromium plating, cadmium plating and nickel plating of steel and brass are carried out; new employees have not been sufficiently instructed in safety procedures. After a month, severe vomiting was observed in a worker "D", the vomit was bluish-green, and the patient died after a few hours. In the preliminary analysis, with 5% K3[Fe(CN)6] and 2% CdCl2 a lilac-coloured precipitate formed, and with the pyridine thiocyanate reagent the chloroform layer was emerald green. Question: which metal was he poisoned with? Indicate the procedure for isolating and analysing the toxic substance.

The "Decision tree" method. First a general problem is posed and three decision options are considered. For each decision option, its advantage and its disadvantage are written. In the end a decision is chosen and justified. This method teaches one to set out a line of thought consistently.

Review questions. Explain, on the basis of chemical reactions, the methods of establishing the identity and quantity of the zinc cation. Show with examples the use of diethyldithiocarbamate salts, that is, DDTC, in the fractional analysis of metal cations. Explain the reasons for extracting with toluene the compound of the antimony cation with malachite green. Explain, on the basis of chemical reactions, the methods of establishing the identity of the thallium cation.

General review questions. Indicate, with 3-4 reactions, the organic reagents used in separating metal cations and in establishing their identity and quantity. Show, using cations as examples, the use of DDTC salts in the fractional analysis of metal cations. Write the chemical equations of the reactions. How is the need to determine the quantity of metallic poisons in forensic chemical examinations explained? Explain with examples the use of dithizone in detecting toxicologically significant metal cations.

Review questions on zinc and bismuth. Explain, on the basis of chemical reactions, the methods of establishing the identity and quantity of the zinc cation. Explain the methods and conditions for separating the zinc cation from other metal cations. How is the bismuth cation detected by the fractional method? Which reactions are considered principal, and which additional, in detecting bismuth in the mineralisate? Indicate the methods of determining the quantity of the bismuth cation.

Review questions on antimony and thallium. Which reactions are used in the fractional detection of the antimony cation? Explain the reasons for extracting with toluene the compound of antimony with malachite green. For what purpose is a nitrite salt added to the mixture in detecting antimony with malachite green? Explain, on the basis of chemical reactions, the methods of establishing the identity of the thallium cation. Indicate the methods of determining the quantity of thallium and antimony cations.

Safety and working procedure. In the reactions, chloroform, toluene, 40% sulphuric acid, 5N HCl, sodium hydroxide and ammonia are used, so caution is necessary. Vigorous shaking is carried out in a separatory funnel; in separating cadmium the shaking lasts 30 minutes. The analysis is conducted strictly by pH and volumes, with the help of universal indicator.

Reaction equations and interpretation tasks. For each of the reactions of thallium, zinc, antimony and cadmium, a chemical equation must be written. For zinc, an interpretation is given according to the requirements of forensic chemical analysis, based on the reaction results. The result of the antimony sulphide reaction is likewise interpreted according to the requirements of forensic chemical analysis. The shape of the microcrystals is drawn in the laboratory notebook.

Recording the result. Having found the solution to the situational problem, it is properly recorded in the laboratory notebook. Expected outcome: detection of the antimony and cadmium cations in the filtrate. Remember: if the result of a reaction is not positive, further examination for the corresponding cation is stopped.
